translations.text: Because of the sins that you have committed before God, you are being led captive to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.
And when you enter Babylon, you will remain there many years, a long time, up to seven generations; and after that I will bring you out from there in peace.
But now, behold, in Babylon you will see gods of gold, of silver and of wood, carried on shoulders, which inspire fear among the gentiles.
Beware, therefore, that you [?] do not become like the foreigners, and fear them, and that terror does not seize you because of them.
You will see the crowd before them and behind them, worshipping them. But say in your heart: "It is right to worship you, O Lord."
For my angel is with you, and he will seek out [?] your souls.
For their tongue is polished by a craftsman, and they themselves are covered with gold and silver; they are false [?] and cannot speak.
And as for a virgin who is adorned, they take gold
and make crowns with it for the heads of their gods. Sometimes the priests take gold and silver from their gods and spend it on themselves.
And they give some of it as payment to harlots. And they adorn them with clothing as if they were men, the gods of gold and the gods of silver and of wood.
These cannot save themselves from rust [literally "poison"] or from the devourer [?], even though they are clothed in purple garments.
Their faces are wiped because of the dust of the house, which lies very thick on them.
And one has a sceptre like a man who is a judge of the land, yet it cannot kill anyone who sins against it.
It holds a spear and a [?] (perhaps an axe or dagger) in its right hand, yet it cannot save itself from war or from robbers. From this it is clear that they are not gods; do not fear them.
For just as a clay vessel becomes useless once it is broken,
so are their gods. They are set up in houses, and their eyes are full of dust from the feet of those who come in.

And just as courtyards are fenced around someone who has offended a king, as for one to be handed over to death, so their priests make their houses secure with doors, locks and bolts, so that they are not plundered by robbers.
They light lamps, more than for themselves, yet the gods can see none of them.
They are like the beams [?] of the house, and creeping things of the earth lick [?] at their hearts, as they say of gods [?]. These things eat them and their clothing, and they do not feel it.
Their faces are blackened by the smoke of the house that settles on their bodies,
and bats fly over their heads, along with swallows and birds, and likewise cats [?].
From this you may understand that they are not gods; do not fear them.
For the gold that they put on them for beauty will not shine unless someone wipes off its tarnish; and even when they were being smelted [?], they did not perceive it.
They are bought at any price, though there is no breath in them.
Having no feet, they are carried on shoulders, showing their own disgrace to people. Let those who serve them be ashamed.

If they fall to the ground, they cannot rise up by themselves. Even if someone sets them upright, they cannot move by themselves, and if they are tipped over, they cannot get up again. Their offerings are set before them as if they were the dead.
Their priests sell their sacrifices for their own use. Their wives also preserve [?] part of it. They give nothing to the poor or to the weak
from their offerings. A menstruating woman and a woman in childbirth touch them first [?]. Know from these things that they are not gods, and do not fear them.
How can they be called gods, when women set offerings before gods of gold, silver and wood?
In their houses their priests sit with torn tunics, their heads and beards shaven, and their heads uncovered.
They come and cry out before their gods, like people at a funeral meal for the dead.
Their priests take some of the gods' garments and use them to clothe their own wives and children.
If someone does them harm, they cannot repay it, and they cannot repay good either. They cannot set up a king or remove one.
In the same way they cannot give riches or silver. If someone makes a vow to them and does not pay it, they cannot demand it from him.
They cannot save a man from death, and they cannot rescue the helpless from the powerful.
They cannot make a blind man see.
They cannot show mercy to a widow or do good to an orphan.
These gods of wood, overlaid with silver and overlaid with gold, are like stones from the mountain, and those who serve them will be put to shame.
How then can anyone think or say that they are gods?
Even the Chaldeans themselves dishonour them. When they see someone who is mute [?] and cannot speak, they bring him to the court [?] and pray as though the gods were able to speak.
But the gods can do nothing for them. They realise this and abandon them, for there is no understanding in them.
The women put cords around themselves, sit by the roads and burn bran as incense.
When a passer-by on the road draws one of them away and she lies with him, she taunts her companion because the companion was not thought as worthy as she was and her cord was not broken.
Everything done for them is false. How can anyone think they are gods, or call them gods?
They are made by carpenters and goldsmiths. They become nothing other than what the craftsmen want to make them.
Even the people who make them do not live long.
How then can the things they make be gods? For they have left lies and disgrace to those who will come after them.
When war and disaster come upon them, the priests discuss with one another where they can hide themselves with the gods.
How can people fail to understand that these are not gods, but things made by human hands, which cannot save them from war or from harm?

For these wooden objects are overlaid with gold and overlaid with silver. After this all the nations will know that they are false, and it will be plain to kings that they are not gods but things made by human hands, and that there is no work of God in them at all.
Who, then, cannot understand that they are not gods?
For they cannot set up a king over the land, nor can they give rain to people.
They cannot judge a case for anyone, nor can they rescue someone who has been wronged. They are powerless.

They are like crows between heaven and earth. When fire falls on the house of the gods made of wood, or overlaid with silver, or overlaid with gold, their priests flee and escape, but the gods themselves burn up in the middle like [?].
They cannot stand against kings and warriors.
How, then, can anyone accept or think that they are gods? The gods of wood, overlaid with silver and overlaid with gold, cannot escape from thieves or from robbers.
Many people strip the gold and silver off them and carry away the clothing they are dressed in, and the gods cannot help themselves.

A king who shows his own courage is better than those false gods. So is a useful vessel in a house, which serves its owner. Even the door of a house is better than those false gods, because it guards whatever is inside. A wooden pillar in a royal palace is also better than those false gods.
For the sun, the moon and the stars shine brightly. They are sent out to serve, and they obey.
In the same way the lightning flashes brightly and can be seen, and the wind likewise spreads out over every place.
When God commands the clouds to go over the whole world, they carry out his command.

In the same way, fire is sent out from above to burn up mountains, hills and forests, and it does what it is commanded. But these gods are not like any one of these things, either in form or in power.
Therefore they are not to be called gods or thought of as gods. They cannot give judgment, nor can they do good to people.
So understand that they are not gods, and do not fear them.
For they can neither curse kings nor bless them.
They cannot show signs in the sky among the nations. They cannot shine like the sun or give light like the moon.
Wild animals are better than they are, because animals can escape into a shelter and look after themselves.
In no way is it evident to us that they are gods. Therefore do not fear them.
For their gods of wood, silver and gold are like a scarecrow in a fruit garden, which guards nothing.
They are also like a thornbush on a garden wall, on which all [?] the birds perch. Likewise their gods of wood, gold and silver are like a corpse thrown out into the darkness.
From the purple and the marble that rot on them you will know that they are not gods. In the end they themselves will be eaten away, and they will be a disgrace in the land.
Better, then, is a righteous man who has no idols, for he will be far from disgrace.
